newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - Croats eye old homes, Serbs fearful in fading enclave.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Croats eye old homes, Serbs fearful in fading enclave.

text.p: Bombed-out ghost towns litter this road in eastern Croatia, haunted by memories of sniper ambushes and forced marches into exile.

Silence and desolation reigned for years here, broken only by an occasional detonating mine or firefight across a tense ceasefire line. But now life is returning in the form of Croats creeping in to glimpse their old homes.

It is a mournful experience made possible by the pending dissolution of Croatia's last separatist Serb enclave. Eastern Slavonia will revert under United Nations supervision to Croatian rule this spring and wartime boundaries are already disintegrating.

In one of many steps towards the "reintegration" of Eastern Slavonia into Croatia proper, U.N. forces have reopened a direct road through a salient of old rebel terrain linking two major towns on the government side of the line.

Croats can now cross transit checkpoints operated by U.N. troops and a transitional Serb-Croat police force to cut their driving time between Osijek and Vinkovci. En route, many are stopping discreetly to inspect homes from which they were driven in 1991.

Ignoring yellow tape strung along roadside homes warning of mines, Stjepan, his wife, sister, mother and son rummage through the dynamited ruins of their house in the village of Antunovac Tenjski and find a handful of family mementos.
They show reporters faded, water-stained snaps of Stjepan's school graduation and wedding. His wife holds up a soup tureen and serving plate -- all souvenirs of a past demolished by war.
"We first saw our house on (Croatian state) TV but it looks far worse in reality, although we hope to move back this year and rebuild it," says Stjepan, who now lives in Osijek.

"Serbs were only 10 percent of the population in Antunovac before the (1991) war but look at the harm they did here. I can hardly imagine Serbs living here again. Our theory is that there are no good Serbs any more."
SERBS DREAD RETRIBUTION WHEN NEIGHBOURS RETURN
Such intolerance, harboured by Croats who suffered from the war, have left many of the enclave's approximately 120,000 Serbs in dread of violent retribution once their old neighbours return.
The U.N. at first allowed Croats to drive the transit road 24 hours a day but closed it at night after some went into nearby Serb-populated hamlets to threaten locals.
Some Serbs have received death threats since telephone and postal links with the enclave were restored last year.

A U.N. Security Council decision in late January rejecting Serb demands for an autonomous single district was the final straw for some Serbs. Hundreds of families have since left for Serbia in what may be the start of an exodus.

More than 40,000 others have indicated that they will stay by obtaining Croatian citizenship papers to test the nationalist Zagreb government's promise of significant minority rights, including senior ministerial posts.

But Serb leaders predict at least 50-60 percent of their people will flee across the nearby Danube river border to Serbia, convinced that Croatian assurances, made only after sustained Western diplomatic pressure, are not sincere.

U.N. officials estimate only 15-20 percent will go, mainly those with "guilty consciences" -- involvement in atrocities and the expulsion of Croats who were the majority community when war broke out over Croatia's secession from federal Yugoslavia.

The U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES) believes a mixed Croat-Serb police force now in place and a long-term presence of Western monitors will ensure Serb inhabitants can live in reasonable security once 5,000 U.N. troops leave in July.
UNTAES feels some of the early panic and flight has been caused by Zagreb's failure to publish a final list of suspected Serb war criminals to be excluded from a war amnesty.
On February 17, UNTAES won a commitment from President Franjo Tudjman to release such a list quickly. This would help persuade Serb men that they will not be subject to random arrest.
SERB DEMONSTRATIONS

Meanwhile, diehard Serb separatists stage regular demonstrations in Vukovar, the Danube port demolished in an infamous Serb siege, and other enclave communities especially those filled with embittered Serb war refugees from elsewhere.

In Mirkovci, a Serb nationalist hotbed just one km from the Croatian line, brooding and burly men and powdered women gather for weekend protest rallies where emotions are aroused by strident folk music.

"Serbs everywhere, you must be united to survive," wails the singer at one rally. Protest banners are draped across the stage. One says, "The U.N. Is Working For The Croats", another, "U.N. -- Are You Thinking Of YOUR Children?"
"We think they will destroy their homes if they leave," says Chandra Ramesh, a U.N. civil police officer in Mirkovci.
The Croatian government has accused Serbs of laying waste to Croat property ahead of the enclave's handover by stripping buildings and removing the contents to Serbia.
U.N. officials say the problem is minor but concede there is no way to catch every plunderer.
Jovica Nikolic, 35, who fought with Serb rebels in 1991, was loading bricks from a devastated house in an unpatrolled Vukovar side street into a truck.
He said he needed them to repair his home in another part of town which had burned down in the fighting. He could not explain why his truck bore the number plates of Novi Sad, a city in Serbia.

Vukovar remains Croatia's "Stalingrad" long after the shooting stopped. The remains of buildings destroyed by tank and artillery barrages are everywhere. They loom over a teeming outdoor market that is most Serbs' only source of income.
"Maybe nothing was rebuilt because we were never sure which side this region would belong to in the end," mused Radojka Pavlica, a flower vendor in the rutted, muddy main square.
